title: Protestant ground: Decalogue Non facies tibi sculptile—no likeness of heavenly or earthly things to be adored
source_text: XIII. Porro quod Protestantes movet ut sic sentiant expressum est Dei mandatum Decalogo contentum, & saepius in Sacra Scriptura repetitum. Non facies tibi sculptile, neque omnem similitudinem eorum quae sunt in coelo desuper, & quae in terra deorsum, nec eorum quae sunt in aquis, sub terra. Non adorabis ea neque coles. Ubi cum Deus simpliciter vetet ne similitudinem ullam eorum quae sunt in coelo, vel in terra, vel sub terra, adoremus & colamus, inde merito colligunt, imagines Dei, vel Christi, vel Sanctorum in coelis regnantium, nulla adoratione, vel cultu prosequendas esse, ut nec ullas omnino alias; quandoquidem imagines tum Christi, tum Sanctorum, sunt de numero similitudinum, quibus repraesentantur ea quae sunt in coelo, quibus Dei lex omnem cultum abrogat.
pass_a_gloss: Further, what moves the Protestants so to think is the express commandment of God contained in the Decalogue, and often repeated in Holy Scripture. Thou shalt not make for thyself a graven thing, nor any likeness of those things which are in heaven above, and which are on the earth beneath, nor of those which are in the waters, under the earth. Thou shalt not adore them nor cultivate them. Where, since God simply forbids that we adore and cultivate any likeness of those things which are in heaven, or on earth, or under the earth, they gather with desert that the images of God, or of Christ, or of the Saints reigning in the heavens, are to be pursued with no adoration or cult, as neither any others at all; seeing that the images both of Christ and of the Saints are of the number of the likenesses by which those things which are in heaven are represented, from which God’s law abrogates every cult.
pass_b_english: The engine is the Decalogue ban on making and adoring any likeness of heaven, earth, or waters.
Christ’s and the saints’ images are exactly such heavenly likenesses—so the precept strips them of cult.
